newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Low food prices slow down Philippines' CPI growth.
newsitem.headline: Low food prices slow down Philippines' CPI growth.

text.p: Lower food prices dragged down Philippine annual inflation in November to 4.5 percent from 4.7 percent in October, the National Statistics Office said on Thursday.
The inflation announcement, which came just before the stock market opened, sent stock prices soaring as the figure turned out lower than expected.
A Reuter poll of five economists this week had shown the average prediction at 5.7 percent with all participants saying a recent round of local oil price hikes was bound to fuel inflation.
The government itself said last week that November inflation was expected to be between 6.0 and 6.3 percent.
The stock market, which had been drifting in the past few days, reacted to Thursday's announcement by buying blue chips.
By mid-session, the Philippine Stock Exchange index was up by over 40 points, or 1.28 percent, at 3,170.97.

"It's a very good sign ... It should give the market the needed boost. It shows that inflation is controlled even if there's a continued rise in fuel prices," Marco Lucena, an analyst at PrimeEast Securities Ltd, said.
Domestic fuel prices have been on the uptrend since August after the government partially deregulated the industry.
But its effect was offset by falling food prices, thanks to a good harvest, economists said.
In November, the inflation rate for rice was -7.7 percent from -5.3 percent in the previous month. Corn prices were at -1.5 percent from a 4.3 percent increase in October.

As a result, the food, beverages and tobacco index, the heaviest indicator accounting for 58 percent of the overall inflation basket, slowed to 2.0 percent in November from 3.6 percent in the previous month.
Luz Lorenzo, an economist at Peregrine Securities, said expected forthcoming price increases in fuel products was not really a cause for worry.
"Even if we see indirect effects of higher fuel prices on other commodities, these will be very minimal," Lorenzo said.
High petroleum prices were expected to persist as prices in the world market remained firm during the winter season in the northern hemisphere.
The fuel, light and water sub-index went up to 8.5 percent from 7.3 percent in October.
Other sub-indices also rose but most of them were less than one percentage point change from the previous month.
